The Dorcas gazelle (Gazella dorcas) exhibits life-history traits that are finely tuned to the arid environments of North Africa and the Middle East. At the core body temperature typical of active mammals, approximately 38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C], female calves experience a gestation period of 182 days [tg = 182 days] and are born at a wet weight of 1615 grams [Wwb = 1615 grams], and young gazelles are weaned after 82 days since birth [tx = 82 days since birth]. This relatively extended gestation, compared to other small bovids, is thought to facilitate the development of relatively precocial neonates, better equipping them for survival in sparse, predator-rich landscapes. This relatively short suckling period allows the female to recover condition rapidly and prepare for a subsequent reproductive cycle, a critical adaptation in environments where resource availability dictates breeding success.

Sexual maturation in Dorcas gazelles is strongly dimorphic in its timing, a pattern consistent with polygynous mating systems where males delay reproductive investment to prioritize somatic growth. At a stable core temperature of 38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C], female calves attain puberty at an age of 730 days since birth [tp = 730 days since birth]. This allows them to reach a sufficient body size to support the energetic demands of gestation and lactation. In contrast, males, who face intense intraseasonal competition for access to oestrous females, require a longer developmental period to build the body mass and horn size necessary for successful combat. Consequently, male puberty is recorded at an age of 589 days since birth [tp = 589 days since birth] under identical thermal conditions at a temperature of 38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C]. This disparity, with females maturing later in absolute chronological age, underscores a life-history strategy where females prioritize physical readiness for reproduction, while males optimize a trade-off between age at maturity and competitive ability.

Sexual size dimorphism is a pronounced feature of Gazella dorcas, directly influencing the reproductive potential and social dynamics of each sex. The ultimate wet weight, or asymptotic adult body mass, for females is 12,600 grams [Wwi = 12,600 grams], a moderate size that reflects the energetic economy required to sustain a high reproductive output in a xeric habitat. Males, however, attain a considerably larger ultimate wet weight of 16,500 grams [Wwi = 16,500 grams]. This roughly 31% difference in mass is primarily driven by sexual selection for larger body size in males, which confers advantages in male-male combat for breeding territories. Female body mass, while smaller, is still substantial relative to congeneric species, and the 12,600-gram figure (12,600 grams) [Wwi = 12,600 grams] is likely optimized to balance the caloric demands of gestation and lactation against the constraints of a low-quality, high-fiber diet of acacia leaves and grasses.

Reproductive output in the Dorcas gazelle is remarkably constrained, reflecting the ecological realities of an unpredictable, resource-limited environment. At a stable core temperature of 38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C], the maximum annual reproductive rate is achieved through a strategy of producing a single offspring per parturition. Field records indicate that females typically produce just one fawn per litter [N_R_i = one fawn per litter], with a maximum reproductive frequency of roughly one litter each year [F_R_i = roughly one litter each year]. This combination yields a maximum reproductive rate of 1 offspring per year [Ri = 1 offspring per year]. Such a pattern is typical of "slow" life-history strategists, trading the potential for high fecundity for increased investment in each individual offspring, enhancing the probability that the single, relatively precocial calf will survive its perilous first months in the desert.

Maximum longevity in this species represents an extreme commitment to survival in a challenging environment. Under the elevated core body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], which is typical of hyperthermia-prone mammals in desert conditions, the maximum recorded lifespan for Gazella dorcas is approximately 23.7 years [am = approximately 23.7 years]. This remarkable lifespan is exceptionally long for an animal of its body size and is likely facilitated by low extrinsic mortality in well-protected populations and a highly efficient metabolism adapted to water and nutrient scarcity. The fact that individuals can persist for nearly a quarter of a century highlights a life-history strategy heavily skewed toward adult survival, as the slow pace of reproduction means that even minor increases in adult mortality can drastically reduce population viability. This longevity, coupled with late maturation and low fecundity, positions the Dorcas gazelle as a classic example of a species at the extreme slow end of the mammalian fast-slow continuum.
